After 1.d4 c6 2.c4 d5: Originally considered a less-orthodox defence in the Queen's Gambit, this opening has stood as an entire opening system in its own right for decades. The idea behind this defence is straightforward: instead of locking in the light squared bishop on c8, why not support the center with the c-pawn instead?
After 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6: Black develops the knight to its natural square c6, where it controls the centre. This move is sometimes called the old Sicilian.

After 1.e4 e5 2.d4: White plays 2. d4 to smash open the centre. White threatens to take on e5, but really they are provoking exd4, and planning to develop their pieces rapidly by opening up the d-file for their queen and bishop.

concept_note.label: king safety
concept_note.text: Your king is safest behind pawns that haven't moved: each pawn you push in front of it stops guarding squares the enemy pieces can then use for a direct attack, and the pushed pawn itself becomes a target. Castle early, and move those pawns only for a concrete reason, not to stop a pin that isn't there yet.
concept_note.credit: Lasker, Chess Strategy (Project Gutenberg #5614), Chapter VI, The Middle Game: Breaking up the King's Side

Next time, before you put a piece on a square, check whether a pawn can chase it away with a gain of time.

opening.name: Slav Defense
opening.wiki_text: Originally considered a less-orthodox defence in the Queen's Gambit, this opening has stood as an entire opening system in its own right for decades. concept_note.label: holes and outposts
concept_note.text: A hole is a square in your camp that none of your pawns can guard any more; an enemy knight or bishop that settles there can't be chased away by a pawn and usually has to be exchanged. concept_note.label: king safety
concept_note.text: Your king is safest behind pawns that haven't moved: each pawn you push in front of it stops guarding squares the enemy pieces can then use for a direct attack, and the pushed pawn itself becomes a target. Castle early, and move those pawns only for a concrete reason, not to stop a pin that isn't there yet.

concept_note.label: holes and outposts

concept_note.label: passed pawns
concept_note.text: A passed pawn has no enemy pawn in front of it or on the files next to it, so only pieces can stop it, and it grows stronger as pieces come off the board. concept_note.label: pawn structure
concept_note.text: Pawns can't move back, so your pawn structure outlasts almost everything else in the game: an isolated or backward pawn, or doubled pawns that can't protect each other, stay targets long after the moves that made them. Before a pawn move, ask which squares it will stop guarding and whether another pawn can still defend it.

concept_note.text: Your king is safest behind pawns that haven't moved: each pawn you push in front of it stops guarding squares the enemy pieces can then use for a direct attack, and the pushed pawn itself becomes a target. Castle early, and move those pawns only for a concrete reason, not to stop a pin that isn't there yet.

concept_note.label: holes and outposts
concept_note.text: A hole is a square in your camp that none of your pawns can guard any more; an enemy knight or bishop that settles there can't be chased away by a pawn and usually has to be exchanged. Look at which squares a pawn move gives up before you make it, and look for such squares in your opponent's camp as outposts for your own pieces.

concept_note.label: pawn structure
concept_note.text: Pawns can't move back, so your pawn structure outlasts almost everything else in the game: an isolated or backward pawn, or doubled pawns that can't protect each other, stay targets long after the moves that made them. concept_note.label: holes and outposts
concept_note.text: A hole is a square in your camp that none of your pawns can guard any more; an enemy knight or bishop that settles there can't be chased away by a pawn and usually has to be exchanged. concept_note.label: passed pawns

concept_note.label: piece activity
concept_note.text: A piece is worth what it can do: how many squares it reaches matters more than its point value. Put your pieces where they have the most scope, and look for ways to cut an enemy piece off from the fight; a bishop or knight shut out of play is almost a piece less.
concept_note.credit: Lasker, Chess Strategy (Project Gutenberg #5614), Chapter III, General Principles of Chess Strategy: Mobility
